0. MACDONELL (South Toronto). Before the orders of the day are proceeded with, I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) if it is the intention of the government to erect any general federal buildings in the city of Toronto in connection with the erection of municipal buildings there, with a view to having a large public building erected jointly by the Dominion government and the city? Mention has been made of the matter in the ' Globe ' and other papers of Toronto, and if the minister is able to make any statement upon it, I would be very glad if he would do so.

My attention has been called by prominent citizens of Toronto, including Mr. Gourlay, the president of the Board of Trade, to the desirability of considering the question of erecting public buildings, when we do erect them, all upon one of the blocks in that part of the city known, I believe, as ' the Ward.' It is centrally situated, and it has been thought that it would be desirable to place all the public buildings in that locality, but the matter has not been considered by the government for the reason that we have not in contemplation at present the erection of any new buildings in Toronto with the exception of an examining warehouse. It may be that in connection with that building, it would be well to consider this whole subject, but so far that has not been done.
I would like to inquire of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) whether he has had any further communication from Washington under the International Fisheries Treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I have not got any further information on the subject. I have brought the matter, however, to the attention of His Excellency, the Hon. Mr. Bryce, who is going to take up the question with the American authorities.
Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, Mr. BRADBURY.
I want to submit to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) some information on the point as to which I inquired just now, and which it seems to me, should have come to his attention a long time ago through some other channel. I have here a copy of the ' Pacific Fisherman ' of March last, containing a great deal more information regarding the progress, or want of progress, of these regulations at Washington, than apparently has come to the minister. This paper reports that so far from the condition being as indicated by the hon. minister, namely, that the Senate at Washington was simply considering some unimportant changes as to the mesh allowed-so far from that being the limit of the alterations by the Senate, the American Senate on the contrary has already made the most drastic changes in the regulations submitted to that body by the joint commissioners. Let me read for the information of the House the article in the ' Pacific Fisherman.' It is as follows:
The International Fishery Treaty, as framed by David Starr-Jordan and Prof. Edward E. Prince, the two commissioners appointed by the United States and Great Britain to formulate regulations for the control of the boundary fisheries of this country and Canada, was given short shrift by the session of Congress which has just adjourned.
Tile energetic and logical protests which were made against the terms of this treaty by the fishermen of Puget Sound and Lake Erie had sufficient weight with Congress that the regulations proposed for those two districts were entirely stricken out by the Committee on Foreign Relations, to whom the Bill was referred. And even after these objectionable features were removed, the Bill, favourably reported by the committee, owing to the filibustering that was carried on in Congress during the last hours of the session, was never brought to a vote.
The Congressional Record shows that the treaty, which came before Congress in the form" of Senate Bill 6119, was referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations, and that, owing to representations made to this committee, regulations 62, 63, 64 and 65, relating to Puget Sound, were entirely stricken out, as were also regulations 45 to 50 included, relating to Lake Erie. Further records state only that this Bill was 'reported with amendment,' which means that it did not come up for vote.
So far as the future of this treaty is concerned, its fate is problematical. The next Congress will be an entirely new session with many new members. The Bill, if again introduced, must necessarily go through all the routine that it has gone through in the last session. It will probably be handled by the committee in the same manner as before, and then, if Congress finds time, it may be passed. It is more than likely that the same representations made by the fishermen, even to a new committee, will have the effect of eliminating the clauses concerning Puget Sound and Lake Erie, and in this event Pa-
8431 '

cific coast fisheries will have little concern in its further history.
If this be a correct presentation of events in the American Senate-and in the absence of information to the contrary we are entitled to suppose that it is-it seems to indicate an astonishing lack of knowledge on the part of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) of, or control over, the events relating to his department. It is no light matter that a treaty solemnly entered into between the governments of Great Britain and the United States should be implemented by Canada, as we did implement it last session, by taking authority for the minister to proclaim regulations whenever the United States was ready to proclaim them, and yet that the minister in charge of the department in Canada should remain indifferent to the fact that he is being played with by the other parties to the treaty, that not only have they committed a breach of international honour by failing during two sessions of Congress to adopt regulations which they were in honour bound to adopt, but they are guilty of a gross breach of their pledge in now undertaking to strike out important provisions in this Act.
I would recall to the minister the events connected with the long protracted negotiations of the two international commissioners. They have been referred to in this House at various times; and although we have had no formal information from the government on the subject and have had to content ourselves with such scraps as we could extract from time to time, by whatever questions we were permitted to ask, it is admitted that the making of these regulations had been a matter of mutual concession. Canada yielded on one point in order to secure an agreement by the Americans on another. It has been held up to us that one of the most valuable considerations we received for the part we allowed the American government in the control of the fisheries arrangements on the lakes, and the Atlantic, was their consent to regulate fishing on Puget Sound where, under present conditions, Canadian salmon are being wantonly destroyed. It has been held up to us by the Minister of Fisheries particularly that this wTas a most valuable concession to us, that we should overlook on that account many defects in that agreement, and that these regulations should be adopted because it was of so much value to us that we should have regulations in Puget Sound.
But we find that, after we have paid the price of adopting the regulations agreed upon in return for the American promises to regulate the Puget Sound traps, they calmly strike out their regulation of the traps and leave us in the position of having paid a price and getting no return 268
whatever for it. Similarly, no doubt, with regard to Lake Erie. I am not in a position to discuss in detail the effect of striking out these regulations with regard to Lake Erie, but there must be other members of the House who are in a position to point out to the minister wherein the united States gain the advantage by striking out these regulations. It seems to me that the minister is confronted with a most serious duty, the duty of reporting to the other parties to this agreement, that, in an affair of this kind, honour must be observed, and that the time has passed when sharp practice can be indulged in-that this Dominion is not so petty, so inferior, a state that any larges community who have a treaty with us may violate that treaty at their will. They humbug us into making conditions by ottering to give us a price, they accept the conditions and then deny us the price. That appears to be what is in progress iat Washington just now. So tar as we can ascertain our Fisheries Department has paid no attention whatever to the course of these regulations at Washington Only the other day, I inquired of the minister whether alteration was being made m the terms of the regulations. The minister answered in the most indefinite way, with no formal report, with no official statement from Washington to read to the House, and nothing to report except some trifling amendments with respect to the size of mesh of the nets to be used, l would like the minister to explain to the House how it comes that he _ is without information on these very important matters. Is it not possible tor some of his array of officials to follow the course of affairs at Washington, so that the department here and this parliament may be kept advised? Does he consider that when the negotiation is completed his duty is ended? In fact, does not he think that it is the continuing duty of the commissioner especially appointed by the government to follow this treaty through all its ramifications at Washington and to report from day to day or from week to week to the minister, so that he may know what is being done in Congress with the regulations to which he and the government have given their sanction? I would point out further the anomaly of the position in which the minister has placed himself by his course in relation to this treaty compared with the course being followed at Washington. In the Fisheries Committee of this House two years ago I asked the minister that he should have the regulations of the international commission laid before the committee, so that we might examine them, and might call representatives of the fisheries interests to perform for us service similar to the service being performed at

Washington, by the representatives ot the fisheries interests in various portions of the United States. But the minister took the extraordinary position that we were powerless in this matter, that it did not matter to us what was provided in the regulations, that our part with relation to them was merely to affix the stamp of this parliament to them so that they might become law. I brought the matter up again last session, in this House, with the same result. The minister had not learned wisdom from the example ot his contemporaries in the United States, but again told us that it was absolutely impossible that this parliament could, have any control over this matter or pronounce on the text of the regulations. As I said, wye simply gave the minister power to proclaim the regulations as they were. Nowr, it is true that the treaty itself provides that both governments shall adopt the regulations as they are presented by this international commission. It is equally true that the treaty provides that the regulations as framed should not be altered until they have first been proclaimed and we have learned by experience in what respect they should be changed. But if the United States Senate is allowed to vary the terms ot the treaty and of the signed recommendations of the commissioners, why should not the parliament of Canada nave the same privilege. Why should we always remiin in an inferior position, a position which is bound to work to our disadvantage in every arrangement we have with the united states, because we are not allowed to take the initiative in any proposition in connection with joint undertakings, but are allowed simply to scrutinize what is put forward by the United States government, put forward with their inner consciousness of the effect of their well studied propositions, communicated only to one or two officials of our government, while we in this parliament agree to take a leap in the dark, and adopt them as presented, i dissent from the minister's theory that parliament must sit here helpless and allow the interests of the country to be sacrificed to the interests of our neighbours in this connection and in many simitar arrangements that we have with the American government. i would make another appeal to the minister, because it is of the utmost importance to the salmon industry in British Columbia that we should have some form of regulations for trap fishing in Puget Bound. I would also like him to place the matter forcibly before the .British Ambassador at Washington, the official primarily responsible tor this treaty. For, as the correspondence shows he urged Ithej treaty upon this government, with rather more persistence than we snouid like Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
to see, until at last he committed this government to it. If he was so insistent that we should enter into this treaty with the United States, it seems to me we have a claim upon him to be equally insistent in representing to the government of the United States that they must observe' international honour in this matter. That they must regard every undertaking of the treaty, and that if it appears to them that the treaty is so defective las to call for amendment-by the American Senate, or for direction by the Senatte to the American commissioner, the door should be left equally wide open to us, that we might consider these regulations in every detail, take advantage of our experience and have the same right to freedom to make alterations in that treaty as the Americans are assuming, i appeal to the minister whether he will not rouse himself from his lethargy in this m&tter, whether he will not become the master of this item ot his departmental work and see to it that we reassert and resume the control over our fisheries, which in my opinion, we should never have relinquished.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
The subject which the hon. -member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has brought to the attention of the House. I am glad he has given me the opportunity of making some explanations of the situation in regard to this freshwater boundaries fisheries treaty. The treaty was made nearly three years ago, and it provided for the appointment of a commission composed of one man representing the United States and one man representing Canada, Dr. David Starr Jordan was appointed on the American side, and Professor Prince was appointed by Canada. They went to work, and visited the country from one end to the other, and adopted regulations which, though not absolutely drastic, were in the right direction. We must bear in mind that it is, far more difficult for the American authorities to make concessions in the regulations than it is for Canada. The American authorities are to some extent checked by the different states. Those regulations concerning the fisheries were made formerly by the various states interested, and it was expected to be a difficult thing to get the states to agree to certain concessions in the regulations. However, regulations were passed and were accepted by the Canadian government, and also by the United States government, and then they had to be submitted to the United States Senate. It is contended in the United States that the Senate, along with the president, is part of the treaty making power, and consequently the regulations had to be submitted to the Senate. My

hon. friend says that he cannot understand why the treaty had to be submitted to the United States Senate, when it has not to be submitted to the Canadian parliament. This_ makes it necessary for me to point out to him that the cases of the two countries are absolutely different. In Great Britain, under British institutions, the treaty making power is vested in the King. The King can sign any treaty and make it valid without its being submitted to parliament, that is>. any treaty which does not affect Canadian interests.
If the Canadian parliament desired to pass upon that treaty would not that desire be granted by the British government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
The rule in Great Britain, which is also recognized in Canada, is that a treaty which does not affect taxation or commercial relations has not to be submitted to the British parliament. There are treaties made frequently in Great Britain which do not affect taxation or the payment of money, and such treaties can be made by the King without its being necessary to submit them to parliament. When a treaty not affecting taxation or commercial relations is signed by the King, it becomes obligatory throughout the empire. Now the same rule applies to treaties which affect Canada. If it is a treaty which does not concern our commercial relations and which does not require the payment of any money or levy taxation upon the subject, it may be signed by the King, and it immediately becomes operative without the consent of the Canadian parliament. But with other treaties which do affect taxation, a different rule prevails. For instance, take the treaties with France in 1893 and in 1907, those were submitted to the Canadian parliament. So was the treaty with Japan, because it affected taxation. This rule is adopted according to the underlying principle of British institutions that no taxation shall be levied without the consent of parliament.
In the United States the situation is not the same. The President of the United States is not the treaty making power. He negotiates, either through his Secretary of State or by himself directly, but a treaty thus agreed upon has no effect until it is assented to by the Senate of the United States. In respect to treaties, therefore, the United States Senate fulfils the functions which are discharged by the British government. In the United States, the treaty making power being vested in the president and in the Senate conjointly, a treaty must receive the assent of the Senate before it can come into force. There have been several treaties made affecting Canada which have been assented to by the President of the United States, but which 268*
did not receive the assent of the Senate. If I remember rightly, the treaty negotiated in 1873 was accepted by the president, but was not assented to by the Senate, and, therefore, it did not come into force. The same with regard to the treaty of 1888 which was negotiated by Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Bayard; that treaty was signed by the president. and Secretary of State, but it was not assented to by the Senate.
Now with regard to the treaty which is under consideration, it is claimed by the American authorities that the regulations, in order to have force and effect, must be submitted to the treaty making power, namely, the president and the Senate. The president has sent a message to the Senate approving of the regulations under the treaty, with the exception of one clause therein concerning Lake Huron. My hon. friend referred to Lake Erie, but I think he was mistaken. The slight change which was mentioned in the message of the president related to Lake Huron, and not to Lake Erie. It is not, however, a matter of much importance.
The Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate had this subject under consideration and they made a report, I suppose, to the United States Senate. If I am rightly informed these proceedings before the Foreign Relations Committee are generally secret, and I do not know how far the information which my hon. friend has conveyed to the House is correct. But, I think, on the whole it is substantially correct that the United States Senate-or not the United States Senate, because the Senate have not passed judgment upon it-but the Committee on Foreign Relations made a report to the Senate during the last session. As far as the government of the United States are concerned, I mav say to my hon. friend that when I was there last winter I took up the question with the representatives of the Secretary of State, and it was understood that with a little amendment which was suggested concerning the size of the mesh to be used on some part of Lake Huron, the United States government would be willing to accept these regulations. There were also some slight changes in regard to the size of the mesh used on Lake Ontario which was, I think, in the interest of our own fishermen. The United States government have, in so far as I can- see, fulfilled that part of their obligation. It is now only for the United States Senate to pass judgment upon the regulations which are before them. My hon. friend has stated that we are not doing our duty. I think his charge in that respect is absolutely unfounded. Can we interfere with the power of the United States government or the United States Senate to pass judgment upon these regulations, to approve of this treaty or not?

Can we make any remonstrance to the American authorities?

I notice that by article 3 of the original treaty it is provided as follows:
The two governments engage to put into operation and to enforce by legislative action, with as little delay as possible, the regulations, restrictions and provisions, with ap-piopriate penalties, proposed by the commission.
y
That article has been adopted by the United States Senate and by the Dominion of Canada. Does not the minister think that when once the United States Senate has bound itself in honour to abide by the regulations which the commissioners shall make, it ends its executive duties and must, therefore, accept such regulations as were made by the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The information which was given to me by the representatives of the government there, was that they maintain that the treaty-making power in the United States Senate is still in existence with regard to the consideration of these regulations, that it was part of their powers | under the constitution, and that, therefore, the United States government could not force the Senate to take any action.
But the treaty has been made as far as that is concerned, and one of the express terms of the treaty was that they were to abide by the express terms of the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes.
Now, when the commissioners make regulations they are going back and altering those regulations. _ If they have a right to do. that we have a right to do the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The government of the United States have done their part, but the other branch of the treaty-making power have not seen fit to pass judgment upon the treaty or the regulations that are before them.

I think that my hon. friend perhaps has not grasped my meaning.' The very body that is now attempting to amend these regulations-the Senate- is the very body that said previously: We will abide by such regulations as are made by the commission. Now, when they attempt to interfere with these regulations they are going back on the treaty which they formerly made, and if they have a rigfit to say first: ' We will abide by what the commissioners do,' and then turn around and say: 'We will not abide by what they do,' this parliament has a right Mr. BRODEUR.
to do the same thing, and we should have the right now to revise these regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: These regulations are not in force yet in Canada.	.
Was the treaty ratified by the United States Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The first treaty, yes.
Then they have no right in the world to change it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is claimed that they have the power to legislate in jeference, not only to the original document which was signed, but also with reference to the regulations which were to be submitted to them. That is their contention.
Did the minister understand when he asked parliament to ratify these regulations by Act of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, because we were bound by the treaty ourselves. The treaty-making power, as far as we are concerned, lies with the King. When the King signs a treaty of that kind we are bound by it, and we have no right to amend a treaty made by the King.

I understand that perfectly. Apparently I have not made myself plain. The minister asked thi3 parliament to ratify these regulations because His Majesty had agreed by treaty to do that. That is correct, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We simply provided by legislation for the necessary power to carry out these regulations. We did not ratify the treaty. My hon. friend will find that the legislation which was passed last year was not legislation to ratify the treaty, but it ,-was legislation providing two things: First, the necessary money to carry out the regulations, and, secondly, the necessary power for the Department of Marine and Fisheries to carry out the regulations. That is all we passed last year, so that there was no ratification by this parliament of the treaty itself because it was not necessary. The only ratification was by the King, and that treaty having been made by the King we are bound by it. My hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) asks why, under these circumstances, should we not amend our regulations? I have explained that as far as we are concerned we have no right to amend these regulations.

I would like to understand it. I understand that a treaty was ratified by the United States Senate and the British government on our behalf. If that is not so, it is entirely news to me. I understand the treaty has been ratified by both powers providing for the

making of regulations, and that both parties agreed to abide 'by -whatever regula-itons the commission would make.
Mr. ' BRODEUR. Precisely, and the United States government maintain that the United States Senate have the same powers to pass judgment upon these regulations as they had to pass judgment upon the first treaty that -was signed. That is the contention of the American authorities.

Can the minister point to any provision in the treaty which says that, notwithstanding the Senate has delegated it powers to a commission to make regulations, and has agreed to abide by the treaty and to put into operation the regulations made by the minister, it shall -also have the right to -revise its whole action and mutilate the regulations to suit itself?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I am not ready to pass judgment upon the United States constitution. That is a matter for them to decide and it is not a matter for us to decide. I am obliged to take the situation as it is. As far as we are concerned the situation is this: The treaty has been made by the King. It was not necessary that that treaty should be ratified by this parliament because it came into force as far as this country was concerned -willingly or unwillingly.
May I ask the minister if that treaty was not made with the consent and concurrence of this government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Certainly.
Certainly it was.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not want to say that we are not responsible for this treaty. We are responsible for this treaty. The treaty has been made as far as we'are concerned. Now, on the other side, one of the branches of the treaty-making power does not ratify it. My hon. friend says that we should take the necessary steps to make a remonstrance. I do not think it is a case where we should interfere. Our interference, instead of doing good, might do harm. I am afraid that the reflections my hon. friend has to-day cast on the American authorities, instead of helping along this treaty will have a contrary effect.

If the minister said to his deputy minister:	I will abide by
what you do, and in pursuance of that the deputy does something, would the minister have the right to say later on: I shall not abide by what you have done: that is the same position.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is not the same thing at all.
Exactly the same.

I wonder how the minister can be sincere in his statement that he was glad to have an opportunity to explain the situation in respect to this matter, in view of the fact that more than once has he refused to give information on the subject when asked to do so in this House. This treaty was entered into three years ago, and time after time since he has refused to take the House into his confidence upon the plea that it would not be proper to give information until the negotiations were completed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I never refused to give any information that I had. When the regulations were passed I brought them down right away.
I have heard the minister more than once give the curt reply that he could not give that information or bring down the papers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: All the papers are before the House.
Since when?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Long ago.

I heard them refused not very long ago. We are told by the Minister of Finance that we cannot change a word in the reciprocity agreement before the House because the treaty-making power belongs to the mother country and not to us, but still we are supposed to have a say in what commercial treaties are made in our interest. Just as we are advised with regard to the reciprocity treaty so the Minister of Marine tells us that we cannot change a word or an item in these regulations, although on the other hand the United States Senate declare that they are at perfect liberty to change the treaty in any way they please. It seems to me that there is inconsistency there. If we have the right to ratify it surely we have the right to change it.
Mr. BRODEUR, The trouble is that we have not the right to ratify it.

I was speaking with regard to the reciprocity pact, and it seems to me we have the right to change that, and if the United States Senate will not ratify it with the changes we have made they can do just as they like about it. I do not think that the ministers of the Crown set before parliament the clear rights which this parliament enjoys and may exercise. The fishing industry of Canada is of very great importance not only to eastern Canada and western Canada, but to central Canada as well. I represent a district that is very deeply interested in the fishing rights of the Georgian Bay, and the waters

connected therewith. There is a great value involved in our fisheries, not only on account of the money value of the fish themselves, but of the large number of people who are engaged in and connected with the industry, and who have for years been waiting for the government to do something in their behalf. The fisheries will remain a most valuable asset to Canada, and a permanent asset, if they are wisely protected and proper efforts made to replenish them. I hold, Sir, that the government is not showing the live interest in that industry which its importance deserves. The people of Canada think that the government are indifferent and dilatory in the matter and indifference and carelessness on the part of those charged with the responsibility of protecting and replenishing our fisheries will some time or other be punished by the people. We on this side of the House have endeavoured to spur the government on to activity in dealing with our fishing interests, but so far we have not been able to succeed, and the people interested are suffering because of the lethargy of the government. We have unfortunately only a joint national interest in these fisheries, and it behoves us to make the best we can of that joint interest. The ministers took this subject up many years ago, and they have been dabbling with it ever since. It is true that these international affairs move slowly, but I would like now to ask the minister if he can tell me how many years ago it is since the negotiations commenced with the United States government with a view to reaching an amicable understanding as to what should be done for the perpetuation and protection of these fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: If I remember rightly, the question was taken up by the Joint High Commission which sat in 1898 and 1899, and it has been taken up since.

That is in accord with my own imperfect remembrance, that it was taken up 11 or 12 years ago. From time to time various questions have been asked with a view of ascertaining what has been done and with a view of spurring on the government to act with greater alacrity and with a stronger desire to bring these negotiations to a satisfactory conclusion; but we are to-day in practically the same position that we were in many years ago. Our fisheries are being injured and wasted, and they are not being protected or restocked as they should be, either in Canada or the United States. One of the provisions of that treaty was that both parties to the agreement were to exercise their best endeavours to restock these waters as rapidly as possible from year to year. Has that been done? Is Mr. SPROULE.
any attention being paid to it? It is true, we have a few fish hatcheries in our country, and we are endeavouring in a halfhearted and unbusinesslike way to restock these waters; but we are not doing all that could be done. Neither of the contracting parties to that agreement is pretending to live up to it or to carry it out according to its letter and spirit. The treaty was signed in April, 1908. It is now 1911, and nothing has been done yet. That treaty provided that an International Commission should make regulations. That International Commission was appointed, and during the year succeeded in making what they thought were suitable regulations. Those regulations were made two years ago. What has been done in the meantime to carry them out? How many efforts have this government made to induce the American government to bring this matter to a finality? The Minister of Fisheries said: 'When I was in Washington last winter I spoke to them about it.' That is the only evidence we have that he showed any desire or made any effort to have the negotiations brought to such a conclusion that the regulations would be put into operation and carried out. Does that look like interest in what Canada is very much interested in? It seems to me that it does not. Then, certain regulations were to be made by the International Fisheries Commission. They were made, and were signed by David Starr Jordan for the United States and by Prof. Prince for Canada, in May, 1909. Now we are in May, 1911, and during those two years practically nothing has been done on our part. But what has been done by the United States? The Senate have taken the matter up, and in the meantime they have so mutilated and nullified these regulations that they are of little value. I take the regulation with regard to the Great Lakes, which includes the Georgian bay and that part of the country which I represent, and what do I find? I find that the Senate have either repealed or struck out the regulation prohibiting net fishing along the boundary line in Lake Erie. The regulations with regard to the construction of pound nets have also been struck out by the Senate of the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I am not aware that the United States has passed legislation on the subject. Perhaps my hon. friend is better informed in that respect than I am.
The information I have is that they have nullified these regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Not the Senate.
Well, what power has the right to do it except the Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: A committee has reported that to the Senate, hut the Senate, I am informed, has not taken any action.
What I am saying would apply to the committe of the Senate whose duty it is to revise these regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It would not toe fair to the United States Senate to say that they have accepted the committee's report. 1 do not think they have taken any action upon it.

The committee has taken action so far, that they have considered and have failed to agree to these regulations. Therefore, so far as our interest in them is concerned, they are practically dead to us at the present time. Trap nets were prohibited by the regulations, but that regulation is nullified. The regulation prescribing the size of the mesh of the net has been nullified or destroyed also. The regulation regarding the amount of netting that may be done is struck out as well. These regulations on every subject have been practically nullified by that committee. Now, we are told that we are in honour bound to live up to this treaty, which was made on our behalf; that as a nation we have to maintain a high national dignity and are in honour bound to observe it in every respect. But is it not strange that one of the contracting parties is bound toy it, while the other contracting party is at liberty to mutilate in any way they like, cr pay no attention to it? At the same time, we must sit here in silence, and., be told that we have not the information before us, and cannot discuss the matter in this House because the treaty has not yet been dealt with by the Senate of the United States. The information goes out to the people of the United State's, while we are denied the right to inquire into it or debate it in this House. One of the recommendations of the committee is:
It is recommended that the artificial propagation of the various food fishes in the treaty waters be continued by both countries and developed to the fullest possible extent and with the highest possible degree of efficiency. This work is regarded as of vital moment to the preservation and maintenance of the most valuable species of fishes.
Are we living up, to that? Not at all. Is the United States? Not at all. So far as I am informed, no efforts are being made by either country to live up to it. We are treating it as though it were a dead letter. It is true, it is only a recommendation; but it is a recommendation by the commission who made regulations to protect and perpetuate these fishes, and this regulation is considered by them as important for that purpose. Two years have elapsed, and nothing whatever has been done. Why has
not some effort been made on our side to enforce these regulations? Are we to allow these important and valuable fisheries to be gradually depleted, because we cannot get the Americans to act? I think we should show some determination to have these waters protected. The fisheries in Lake Erie and Georgian bay are of great interest to our people. They are of vital interest to the fishermen in that section, and these fishermen desire to get information and know exactly where they stand. Why have we not done anything? Has the minister been as zealous in looking after the interests of the people in that part of the country as he should be? I think not. The United States, he tells us, have not yet finally accepted the treaty and, therefore, we can do nothing. But what has our government done to expedite their acceptance? So far as we know, it has done nothing, and we are denied the right to get information or to detoate this question because the United States Senate has not finally dealt with it. It seems to me that we should be just as free as the United States Senate to. discuss this question, and that it is the duty of the minister to give us every item of information in his possession just as though these regulations had been ratified long ago. We are just as much entitled to that information, and to discuss the matter as we are with regard to the reciprocity pact now before this House.
This matter is in the hands of two parties and we are denied any information regarding it. What is done may be for our benefit or otherwise, but we do not know and are denied the means of finding out until such time as our hands will be tied and we shall have to abide by the agreement no matter what the consequences may be. That is how the representatives of the people are treated in this House, and the situation in which we find ourselves is a very pitiable one. We are told that we are debarred from doing anything at present by a high national code of honour, but the United States have not observed that high code of honour which is to be binding on us. If the other party is not willing to abide by it, are we bound to observe it? We are told that the regulations cannot be amended in any direction' by us, but they can be by the other side. That seems to me very unfair. Is it not about time that we brought this childish play to an end and dealt with this matter in an intelligent, businesslike and courageous way. consistent with our own dignity? The government, however, are committed to a policy of drift. They are willing to let things drift in an indifferent haphazard way from year to year until our fisneries will be destroyed. But were the government to do their duty, they would not allow a mo-

ment longer to pass without seeing that our interests were protected. Has the minister given us any evidence that he has been remonstrating with the United States or submitting to them the great desirability of bringing this thing to a finality? If he has not he should do so without any further delay. In any event he should let us know whether anything is being done. If he is unable or unwilling to do anything, then let the House take hold of the matter and discharge the important duty incumbent on it as a parliament, of looking after the interests of Canada.

I want to get an understanding of this thing. I have been listening to the debate so far and especially to the minister's statement, and I am not quite sure whether I have the facts of the case correctly or not. Suppose we try to get the matter clearly in our minds. A treaty has been made between Great Britain and the United States. There is no doubt about that. That treaty has been ratified by the United States Senate. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, the former treaty has been ratified by the United States, but not the regulations.
I am not asking anything about the regulations. I am asking whether or not a treaty made between Great Britain and the United States has been ratified by the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes.

Then the treaty has been ratified by 'both the powers concerned. If that treaty has been ratified by the United States, and if all the forms of the American constitution have been complied with, and if all that is required by the British constitution has been met, that treaty is binding on both the United States and Great Britain and the latter acting on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, so far as these fisheries are concerned. Then all we have to do is ask what the terms of the treaty are; and if we find certain things as articles in that treaty binding and absolute, neither Great Britain nor the United States has any right to vary these. Either power has the right to ask for a revision of the treaty or, under the terms of the treaty, has the right to denounce it; but until either is done, neither Great Britain nor the United States has anything else to do than live up to the terms of the treaty. The minister will not contravene that position? He says nothing, but I know he could not. A treaty would not be worth the paper on which it is written if, after it had been solemnly agreed to and rati-Mr. SPROULE.
fied, either one or the other could do as it liked with regard to carrying it out.
I want to ask another question. Article first is as follows: [DOT]
The times, seasons and methods of fishing in the waters contiguous to the United States and Canada as specified in article i of this convention, and the nets, engines, gear, apparatus and plant which may be used therein shall be fixed and determined by uniform and common international regulations, restrictions and provisions.
Both powers agreed to that, and to that end agreed to appoint, within three months after this convention is proclaimed, a commission to be known as the International Fisheries Commission, consisting of one person named by each government. Both powers are bound by that and should live up to it.
Article 2. It shall be the duty of the International Commission

Not the duty of the United States government ; not the duty of the British^ government acting by way of the Dominion government; not that, but

-the duty of the International Fisheries Commission, within six months after being named, to prepare a system of uniform and common international regulations for the protection and preservation of the food fishes in each of the waters prescribed in article 4 of this convention, which regulations shall embrace close seasons, limitations as to the character, size and manner of use of nets, engines, gear, apparatus and other appliances; a uniform system of registering by each government in waters where requird for the more convenient regulation of commercial fishing by its own citizens or subjects within its own territorial waters or any such part of such waters; an arrangement for concurrent measures for propagation of fish, and such other provisions and measures as the commission shall deem necessary.
So, it. is not the British parliament, nor the British government, nor the American administration, nor the United States Senate,- which is to do these several things; it is the duty of the International Fisheries Commission to do them, and under the treaty nobody else can do what is laid down there to be done by that commission. Now, the International Fisheries Commission-I want to be sure I am right -has met, has agreed upon these regulations, and has reported these regulations to the two governments? I am correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes.

Very well, they have done their duty. Now, what, does article 3 my?
Article 3. The two governments engage to put into operation and to enforce by legislation and executive action, with as little delay as possible-

What?
-the regulations, restrictions and provisions with appropriate penalties for all breaches thereof; and the date when they shall be put into operation shall be fixed by the concurrent proclamations of the Governor General of the Dominion of Canada in Council and of the President of the United States.
The Senate has nothing to do with regulations. The Senate, when it ratified that treaty made its last utterance on these regulations

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: But-

Wait a moment; let me finish my argument-made its last utterance on these regulations when it solemnly agreed, by the two-thirds majority necessary under their constitution, to put the matter into the hands of the International Fisheries Commission. When it did that, it divested itself of all authority in changing or making any of these regulations. They made an article of the treaty which provided how the regulations were to be brought into force. That is, the two governments were to bring them into force by proclamation-not proclamation of the Senate of the United States, or of this parliament, but proclamation of the President of the United States, and of the Governor General of the Dominion of Canada in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: After the legislation being passed.
What legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is mentioned in the clause the hon. gentleman read. It required some legislation to be passed by the United States authorities.
For what purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: For this purpose: The administration of the fisheries was formerly under the control of the different states of the United States. By the treaty which was made concerning these boundary waters, these waters passed under federal control. It required, then, some legislation on the part of the federal authorities to carry out these regulations. It required also an appropriation of money.

That does not throw any light on the subject we were discussing, nor has it anything to do with the matter. What we were discussing, and what was brought up by my hon. friend from New Westminster was that regulations provided for under the treaty, and made by the International Fisheries Commission are proposed to be changed by the United States Senate. The two governments are not to make or alter regulations, but only to put into operation the regulations made by the International Commission. It is not
to be understood or allowed that the Senate should change the regulations made by the commission. But then comes in what the minister has been talking about-that in order to have proper legislation for the enforcement, the administration is to have regard to the different states that have rights and powers in the matter, and to endeavour to get a unitv of enforcement. Does the minister contend that that provides that the Senate of the United States, the body that ratified the treaty may go back upon the regulations which were made by the International Commission and change these regulations? I do not think he can pretend that. Now, have these regulations been put in operation by concurrent proclamation, or have they not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, they have not been.
There is, therefore, no proclamation and consequently up to this time, the regulations made by the International Fisheries Commission are a dead letter. That is where the matter stands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes.

Now, what seems to me the unwarranted thing-and I say that with all due respect-is that a committee of the Senate of the United States, evidently with the idea of bringing up the regulations before the Senate for amendment after proposing changes in these regulations themselves. That is quite open to the Senate, and this treaty is torn into ribbons. There is here a provision by which a revision of these shall be made, if they are not satisfactory. Article 5 says:
The International Fisheries Commission shall continue in existence so long as this convention shall be in force, and each government shall have the power to fill, and shall fill from time to time, any vacancy which may occur in its representation on the commission. Each government shall pay its own commissioner, and any joint expenses shall he paid by the two governments in equal moieties.
The next section deals with a change of opinion which might occur with either of the parties:
The regulations, restrictions and provisions provided for in this convention

Namely, those made by the International Fisheries Commission, not by the Senate, not by the Dominion of Canada, but by the International Fisheries Commission.
-shall remain in force for a period of four years from the date of their executive promulgation-
So that after the executives promulgate ' these, there is no power to destroy this convention, and those regulations remain for a period of four years.

-and thereafter until one year from the date when either the government of Great Britain or of the United States shall give notice to the other of its desire for their revision.
, There is where you have a chance for revision. After these remain in power for four years, if one power says, ' we do not like them, notice is given, and they may be revised, and then the Senate may have something to say about it.' Either one of the contracting parties may refuse to abide by such regulations, and in such a case the treaty will become of no effect. '

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says the matter could be referred to the Senate. I call his attention to the fact that this particular clause simply speaks of * the governments.' I would not like to admit just now that the United States Senate would have the right even to revise, because the treaty simply speaks of ' the governments.'

And thereafter until one year from the date when either the government of Great Britain or of the United States shall give notice to the other of its desire for their revision-
Then revision can commence.
-and immediately upon such notice being given the commission shall proceed to make a revision thereof.
Not the Senate. My hon. friend is quite right. The Senate even then has no power to revise.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It would be a question whether, in such a case, the Senate would have the right. It has been contended by the American authorities, and it has been so stated to me by them, that in every case under these different sections where the action of the government is involved or required, this action is to be exercised, not by the government alone, as we understand it here, by the president and his cabinet, but with the concurrence of the United States Senate. That is their contention.
Even suppose that contention is correct

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I do not say it is correct, but that is their contention.
Mr. FOSTER-the time has not arrived for that, and will not until four years after the promulgation.
Immediately upon such notice being given, the commission shall proceed to make a revision thereof, which revised regulations, if adopted and promulgated by the Governor General of Canada in Council and by the President of the United States, shall remain in force for another period of four years and thereafter until one year from the date when Mr. FOSTER.
a further notice of revision is given as above provided in this article.
' If there be a revision by that International Fisheries Commission, which revision, if agreed to by the two executives, must then be promulgated, the Senate may then put in a claim that they are to advise the president as to whether he shall agree, and they may exercise their right in that advice. But until four years after the promulgation of this set of regulations which has been made by the International Fisheries Commission, the Senate does not seem to me to have lost power under this treaty to alter, change or interfere in any way with those regulations.
It shall, however, be in the power of the two governments, by joint or concurrent action upon the recommendation of the commission to make modifications at any time in the regulations.
To make modifications at any time in the regulations. That they can not do on their own initiative, it must be on the recommendation of the commission alone. So it seems to me that under the present condition of things the minister's stand is not a clear one. He has failed to inform us that he has taken objection to the contention of the United States authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend that when this matter was brought to the attention of Mr. Bryce and myself, who were there together, we understood that in speaking of ' government,' the word meant what we understand it to mean here. But we were informed by the counsel of the Secretary of State, that in such a question it would require not only the action of the government, but the action of the Senate, because the Senate was a part of the treaty-making power.
That is in case of revision. But there is no chance for revision until four years shall have passed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: But then action can only be taken after the proclamation, according to section 3.

Well, I have given the articles in the treaty, and they are as plain as words can be, and it seems to me they leave us in an unsatisfactory position. Of course, the minister may say that these regulations have not yet gone into effect on either side, and consequently they are not operative. But the sole reason of the treaty was to get at an understanding, and to provide a machinery which would protect the fisheries, and keep that inestimable resource of both countries in good condition, and prevent depletion of what is so great a source of food for the people of both countries. My hon. friend from Grey stated that here you have three full years

after the treaty has been made, and you have not yet had the official proclamation of these regulations

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
It is not our fault. .
Mr. FOSTER-and as a consequence of that, you have a hesitation and loss in the fisheries.

I would like to say one or two words. Let me state at the outset that 1 would not presume lor a moment to interpret tne constitution ot tne United States contrary to the views of those who make it their study. What I say, therefore, must be taken subject to the consideration that tne constitutional lawyers of the United States must be presumed to understand their own constitution, and that -what we say in regard to it is only our own understanding ot tne meaning of the language. It seems to me that when the United States Senate ratified this treaty, then the treaty became just as binding upon the United States as it was binding upon Canada by tne ratinca-tion of His Majesty the King. I would ' have thought that, under the circumstances, the regulations themselves would not become subject to the ratification of the Senate except in so far as the treaty lt-self plainly stated that such ratification was to take place. For example, it might be that at the end of the four year period such ratification for a further period might be necessary under the terms of the treaty. What did the treaty amount to? It simply amounted to this, that the government of Canada, through His Majesty the King, and the government of the United States' entered into a treaty by which they agreed that these regulations should be according to the arbitrament and decision of the tribunal which the treaty appointed. That is the meaning ot the treaty it it means anything. After these regulations have been made by the duly constituted tribunal it is said that the Senate of the United States claims the right under its treatymaking powers to revise them. I do not know whether 1 am correct in that. The Senate of the United States might interfere in two ways. It might interfere, as one of the legislative bodies of the United States, by declining to pass legislation enforcing these regulations unless some amendment were made in the regulations themselves. It would possess that power, and it could exercise that power, although such exercise would not be in accordance with the terms of the treaty, just the same as this parliament might decline to implement the treaty that had been made. That is one thing, but that is not what I understand is being done at the present time. The Senate of the United States is not interfering in that way, but it is interfering
under that clause of the constitution which vests in the Senate a portion of the treatymaking power of the United States. _ It does not seem to me conceivable, subject to the superior wisdom of the constitutional lawyers of the United States, that that particular thing would be possible. Let me illustrate. Suppose the Unitei States and Great Britain entered into a treaty by which they referred claims by the United States against Great Britain, or by Great Britain against the United States, to the arbitrament and determination of a particular tribunal. Such a treaty would not be binding upon the united States until it had been ratitlei by the Senate in accordance with the provisions of their constitution, but after it had been once ratified, it would be thoroughly binding upon the United States, and it would be imposible for the Senate of the United States, after the award had been made by the tribunal to which these claims had been referred, to say: We have now the right, under the treaty-making powers of the constitution, to vary and alter that award. If it could not do that, and it is plain to me that it could not, in the case of the arbitration by which 1 have illustrated my argument, then it seems to me equally impossible that it should do so in the case which the minister has brought to the attention of the House to-day. I would like to ask, in conclusion, from the minister, whether it is by virtue of the ordinary legislative power of the Senate, or whether it is by virtue of the treaty-making power of the Senate, that these regulations are now alleged to he subject to modification?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is the point upon which I have no definite information, but I assume, by reason of the message which was sent to' the Senate, that it is being dealt with under the treaty-making power. I am under the impression that that is the way in which it is being dealt with, because the matter has been referred to a committee on foreign relations, and I would, therefore, be inclined to think that the Senate has been acting in its capacity as a part of the treaty-making power. But, as I have said, I have no definite information on that point.
Has the minister the resolution which was introduced in the Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I think we have. I think it was sent to the department by the British ambassador. I may inform the House that this morning I discussed this question with Mr. Bryce myself.
Mr. Speaker, this matter has been discussed in this House on more than one occasion, and I think its importance is sufficient warrant for the discussion which has heretofore taken place. The

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That question was not considered at all at the time.

Then I may gather from that, that the minister is as _ much surprised at the action of the United States Senate in that connection as are other members of this House. I assume that if the minister had known that the United States Senate were going to revise the action of the commissioners, he would have imparted that information to the House two years ago, when this matter was discussed; and the very fact that it was not understood is an evidence of the other undoubted fact, that all our dealings with the United States are entered into without a full and complete knowledge of where they

are going to land us. I think in matters of such vital importance as this-important to the fisheries and important to the people interested in the fisheries-there should be no room for misunderstanding; and that when this country agrees to a treaty entered into by Great Britain on our behalf with the United States, it should be with a knowledge of where that treaty is going to lead us, where it is going to leave us, and what we are going to get under it.
Now, so far as we are concerned, these regulations, I presume, cannot be reviewed. I will ask the. minister, however, whether or not, in view of the situation which has unexpectedly developed in the United States, we can give to our commissioner, or, if not, to his department, or, if not to his department, then has this parliament, the right also to make changes and alterations in these regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: There is no doubt that under the treaty the regulations might be revised with the consent of this government and the treaty-making power of the United States.
Then may I ask the minister if he is giving consent to the alterations which are being imposed by the United States Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Certainly not. I may say, however, with regard to one of the changes, concerning part of Lake Huron which is a result of a difference in the size of the mesh, I stated to the American authorities that we would have no objection to have an amendment made; but it was of no importance.

Then we reach this conclusion, that while we on this side of the herder can only make changes in these regulations with the consent of the United States Senate, they on the other side of the border can mutilate or alter them in any -way they choose without obtaining the consent either of the government of Canada or of this parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: But the amendment could not be put in force except with the consent of the Canadian government.
I can quite understand that, but in this case they are not proposing to add to, but are striking out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The same thing.

Not exactly the same thing. Consequently we would have a skeletonized form of these regulations, none of the remaining regulations, perhaps, being objectionable to us, and yet the form and substance of them, necessary in order that the fisheries should be conserved, being stricken out. So that I do not suppose that

the minister will say at this moment that if these changes, which have been recommended by a Committee of the United States Senate, are made by the Senate, he will take the responsibility of refusing to pioclaim the regulations in force in this country. Perhaps the minister may have reached that conclusion, and, if so, will state it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, I have not considered that point at all.

That certainly indicates a very unfortunate position for Canada, for Canadian fishermen, and for the people of this country generally. Can the minister state at this time in what stage the regulations are in the United States Senate, or whether they have yet been submitted to the new Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not know whether they have been submitted this session or not. I do not think they have.

I gather from what the minister says that the government on this side of the line have practicaly decided to abandon the regulations, as they do not seem to be in touch with the United States Senate. When the regulations come back here, they may be in such a skeletonized ferm that they will be simply worthless, as I think they are now. Consequently the advantages which we had hoped at one time we would get under properly-framed regulations, will be lost to the people of this country and to our fisheries. In my view, there is in this matter a question of international faith at stake. I believe that we should adopt a firmer policy in our dealings with the United States. I do not think we should consent to have them trifling with the administration of this country. It seems to me that they consider the government of Canada to be a pretty easy mark, from the manner in which they have been conducting themselves with respect to these regulations; and almost every other case in which we have had dealings with them of late, has indicated a similar disposition on their part and a similar state of mind on the part of the government of that country. In the meantime, the question is, how are we going to protect and conserve the fisheries which were to be protected under these regulations? It seems to me that the whole thing has so far fallen to the ground. It is a most regrettable thing that matters should have reached the stage at which they are.
I trust that the government will take the very earliest opportunity to see that whatever is going to. toe done under this treaty, in connection with these regulations, is done, and is reported promptly to this parliament, and that any rights wjiich

we may have under that treaty are preserved to the people of this country.

I would like to ask the minister whether or not legislative action is required for the purpose of putting into operation these regulations? If so, whether or not the ratification by the United States Senate can be considered as legislative action on the part of the United States or whether ratification is required by both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Article 3 of the treaty reads:
The two governments engage to put into operation and to enforce by legislation and executive action the regulations.
The United States Senate have passed an Act (ratifying the regulations subject to these changes they are making. I desire to know whether or not that is legislative action as required by the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not know whether the United States Senate, in considering these regulations, has acted by virtue of its jurisdiction as a branch of the treatymaking power.
Does the hon. minister know whether the House of Representatives has sanctioned the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, it has not.

This article says that the regulations require to be sanctioned by legislative action, and 1 would assume that means legislation "by both Houses. It is the intention that these regulations, after going through the Senate, shall go to the House of Representatives for legislative sanction?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The official information that I have is that a message was to be sent by the President of the United States recommending the necessary legislation and the adoption of regulations. I have no other information on the subject.
Does the minister know whether or not the British House of Commons has taken legislative action?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No legislative action was required on the part of the British authorities because the matter concerned Canada alone. It was contemplated in the treaty that the legislation mentioned in article 3 should be passed by the Dominion parliament, and that has been done.
So far as Canada is concerned, evidently we are absolutely bound by the regulations passed by the joint commissioners and the United States are not.
Nobody is bound to-day, because no final action has been taken and no proclamation has been issued.
Suppose Congress should pass the regulations mutilated as they are, would we be bound by them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Certainly not. It would be for us to consider whether those amendments should be accepted or not.
Who would have the power to alter the regulation's-the commission or this government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is provided in the treaty that the regulations may be revised by the two governments on the recommendation of the commission. It would be for this government to decide whether there was such a recommendation on the part of the commissioners.

The hon. minister knows that such recommendation can only be made after four years. I think it is time this House should protest against being placed in the unfair position in which we aTe. That position seems to be that while the United States agreed to abide by whatever regulations might be made by this commission, and while we agreed to be 'similarly bound, yet the United States Senate is now mutilating these regulations to suit itself. Both countries having delegated their powers to that commission to make those regulations, all that remained to be done was to ratify them and neither country had any power to amend,_yet we find the United States Senate amending the regulations to suit themselves. I want to protest against another thing in connection with this treaty, and that is this. Apparently the United States make public the contents of the treaties long before we have any information here as to what is contained in them. In the present instance these regulations made by the Joint Commission, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows, were published and sent broadcast throughout the United States long before we in Canada knew anything about them. I had a copy of the regulations from an outside source long before I could procure them from this government. Then take the other case, that of the International Commission which it is proposed to establish and place in charge of railway rates, express rates, telephone rates and telegraph Tates. Down to this day, we have no information from the government regarding the contents of the report on this subject. I asked for that information three months ago, but so far we have neyer had any information of what that report contained. The matter is a very important one, the establishment of an International Commission to regulate international railway rates, express, telephone and telegraph rates. Yet although we have no information from this government and none can

be obtained from it, there appeared three months ago in the American ' Review of Reviews ' a full exposition of the contents of that report. The ' Review of Reviews ' went on to state this:
It is expected that with the reciprocity treaty there will also he submitted to Congress the text of some sort of traffic agreement with Canada to regulate the railroad business over the border. . . . The report of Chairman Knapp, concurred in by Chairman Ma-bee, and presented to the Secretary of State on the last day of December, contains recommendations of such importance to those of our citizens who are interested in trade and travel across the border that we herewith summarize its most important points.
The writer of that article, as far back as last February, went on to summarize and give details of the contents of that report which our Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) said the other evening had not been divulged and that he was not at liberty to say anything about it. Notwithstanding the statement, this report was published last February in the ' Review of Reviews.' The article goes on to say:
The proposed treaty provides for a tribunal to enforce and administer its provisions to be known as the International Commerce Commission, and which shall consist of four members, namely, the chairman of the Interstate Commerce Commission and the chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada for the time being, a member of the Interstate Commerce Commission to be appointed by the President of the United (States, and a member of the Railway Commissioners of Canada to be appointed by the Governor General of Canada in Council. The powers conferred upon and the authority given to this commission in respect of international carriers would correspond to those exercised by the Interstate Commerce Commission in respect of interstate carriers within the United States.
The provisions of such a treaty should apply to telegraph, telephone and express companies and such companies should be subject as respect to international business to the authority of the International Commerce Commission.
Then it goes on to give other particulars. What I want to emphasize more particularly is this, that while we on this side are prepared to preserve secrecy regarding *state documents, commissions or agreements, on the other side they are made public at once: and in that way they get an advantage over us with respect to treaties of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: With regard to the regulations which have been passed, I am not aware that the American authorities published them in advance.

I myself saw a copy of these proposed regulations. It came into Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
my possession from a fisherman in my locality who got it from an American fisherman. That was the first intimation I had of what' these regulations were.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That must be a mistake. I may state what actually occurred in that connection. Professor Starr Jordan sent a draft prepared by himself to be considered by the different states interested. This draft, for reasons unknown, was published by the Ontario government as an official document, but it did not contain the official regulations which were adopted later on, as absolutely different ones were adopted.

They were draft regulations, and the copy I had was marked confidential, yet it was being circulated throughout the United States. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) says they were published in the press of the state of Washington.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: But they are not the regulations adopted later on by the commission. It was merely a draft which was sent out by Dr. Starr Jordan, but which was not accepted by the commission.

That is exactly what we complain of. The draft of the regulations was sent all through the United States to receive the approval or disapproval of their fishermen, before we had the draft here, or an opportunity to consult our fishermen or to receive the advice of our own commissioner.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If I understand the matter, my hon. friend finds fault with us because the results of the negotiations that we had with our American neighbours were disclosed by the American authorities and were not disclosed by us. That is the point the hon. gentleman makes against us. Let me tell my hon. friend that the American system is to divulge everything in matters of diplomacy even before they have got through, while the British system is to disclose nothing until the agreement has been put through, and the thing has become official by the signature of the parties. My hon. friend apparently, has a weakness for the American system:	If I understand aright, he
