would change the British for the American system. But we do not want to do that, either on this occasion or on any other. We are not in favour of annexation; we want to remain British. I think my hon. friend ought not to try to induce us to go out of our way to favour the adoption of American methods.

We do not want reciprocity in that kind of conduct. But if it is the custom of the American government to disclose these documents contrary to the

British system, it is the duty of our government to get the information from the United States as quickiy as possible after they publish it so that we may be in as good a position as they are in that regard. These regulations, I understand, weTe a compromise. The commissioners of the two countries sat down together and eventually agreed upon a certain set of regulations. Now, the compromise is being taken up by the United States Senate, and they are proceeding to amend it to suit themselves, as I contend, in direct contradiction of the terms of the treaty.

I do not know that the information has been given to the House, but as I have not the information, I would like to ask a question either of the Prime Minister or of the Minister of Railways. What authority was ever given to Chairman Mabee that led to his conference with Mr. Knapp? Was it a mere conference of gpod neighbourhood, or was there official direction and instruction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say at the moment, but my impression is that it was a purely friendly conference to ascertain whether the two countries could agree on a common system of that kind.
And not authorized by the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I could not say positively, for I do not remember-at-the moment, but I could ascertain.

speakeroldname: Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia and Defence).
speechtext:
I have distributed for the information of the committee a memorandum which gives a pretty full explanation of the different items making up these main estimates. Perhaps it would be well for me to say a few words generally before proceeding to the items, and in doing so I will detain the committee but a few minutes. It is well known that in June last Canada was visited by one of the principal military authorities in the British Empire, Sir John French, the Inspector General of the British forces, who came here in accordance with an arrangement, I might say an understanding, made as long ago as 1902, when the Canadian



8515
ministers were in England attending the Colonial Conference, as it was then called. They sent a memorandum to the Colonial Secretary indicating the course which Canada was prepared to take with reference to matters of defence, and pointing out that so far as military defence was concerned, we would be glad to have the benefit from time to time of an inspection of the Canadian forces by a distinguished British general. This is the first opportunity since that time that we have had the advantage of such an inspection.
Now, I am not going fully into the report of Sir John French, as no doubt questions will be asked as the different items are under consideration. But on the fourteenth page of the memorandum which has been laid before the members, special reference is made to recommendations of Sir John French, the Inspector General of the British forces, and I wish to confine my observations at the moment to the two points especially referred to in the memorandum. First, the question of organization, secondly, the training and education of the officers and the force generally. I may perhaps observe that Sir Jphn French, being Inspector General of the forces of the empire, and being a soldier and a great general, naturally looks at all troops which he inspects from the point of view of efficiency as an armed force ready for active service. That was his point of view, and natural!'* perhaps, he was to some extent disappointed, or at any Tate would be disappointed, with the Canadian militia as a force of that kind. We in Canada know perfectly well that the Canadian militia has never been a force ready to go to war, that has not been the principal idea in its organization. In fact it is only within a very short time, three or four years, that any such idea would have been suggested in connection with the militia. The purpose of the militia has been to aid, to assist, the British army when difficulties occurred in Canada. The British authorities have always maintained in Canada British forces in different portions of the country up to a very short time ago. In 1905 the last of the British troops were withdrawn from this country, from Halifax and Esquimalt, and Canada then assumed the direct responsibility for the defence of her own territory, thereby relieving the British taxpayer from responsibility in that connection. Previous to that time, while a British force was maintained in CAnada. the Canadian government did not pretend to keep up many of the administrative branches of an army. There was always at Halifax or at Esquimalt the nucleus of an army which could supply, when required, the necessary administrative branches After the troops were with-Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
drawn from Halifax_ and Esquimalt, or about that time, it became necessary for the Canadian militia to organize the different administrative services, and that has been done, so that to-day in that respect, and in every respect, to some extent at least, we have in Canada a force able to take the field if necessary.
I was saying that Sir John French would naturally be disappointed if he expected to find a force absolutely ready to take the field for active service. We did not expect that, he probably did not expect it. But he was asked to make a frank criticism and report of what he found, and of the remedilesi which he woujd suggest, and that I am happy to say he has done. I may say that his report is very satisfactory indeed to the military men of Canada. General Lake, who was here at the time, felt quite satisfied with Sir John French's criticisms. One of the recommendations, or one of the criticisms perhaps I had better say, which Sir John French made, was that our organization was not what it ought to be, that is to say, he found that our peace organization was not such as would lend itself to the best efficiency if the force were ever required to take the field. If we are maintaining a military force at all it must be with a view of having it prepared in the event-much as we would regret it and unlikely as it may be -of war, but still a force which would be fit to take the field if required. The objection which he has made was that the different branches of the force were scattered, that there was not a proper balance in the strength of the different branches as between infantry, artillery, and cavalry, and he recommended that instead of the large commands and the districts which we have had for many years-long before I came into office-we should have divisions established, and that each division should contain within itself all the branches including infantry, cavalry, artillery and the administrative services of the army sufficient to defend completely the particular portion of the country included in the division. This proposal, fortunately, can be carried out without any serious difficulty and I will read here the words of the memorandum which are, as a matter of fact, the words of the present general who succeeded Sir Percy Lake-Major General Mackenzie.
This reorganization can he effected with, practically no dislocation of the existing system, as each divisional command will include one or more of the present military districts. The result of this change will be to place1 under each divisional commander the troops to form the division he would command on mobilization and tend to associate, during training, the units which would work together as a division in the field.

I do not know that I need enlarge at all upon that.
How many districts are there now?
Thirteen. But I may say by way of explanation that Oeneral French has separated eastern Canada from what he calls western Canada, m his report.
What is the line of division?

It is the
lakes. He proposes to 'leave western Canada under the districts as they are at present. The particular organization of which I am now speaking refers exclusively to eastern Canada, that is Ontario, or most of it, Quebec and the maritime provinces.
How many divisional commands are there?

There will be six divisions in eastern Canada. At the present time there are ten districts so that it really means a diminution in the number.
Mr- DANIEL. Will the minister give the boundaries of the different divisional commands of eastern Canada while he is on the subject?

Yes. There will be three divisions in Ontario. One of these divisions will include two military districts. The province of Quebec is also divided into two divisions in place of the three districts which now separate the different parts of the province. The maritime provinces will be one division. As a matter of fact at the present time they are put under one larger command, but they are divided, and have been for many years into three districts.

In the divisional Command are all the officers who administer that division in the time of peace assembled at headquarters, or are there some remaining as they have been in different places, say in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick?
No, a'll the staff officers are at the head of the division.
They will all be removed to Halifax then?
What form will that instruction take?
It is being carried out now, and we hope that during the present financial year it will be in full operation.
The officers of the permanent force are held at the disposal of the department to do this work?
Yes,
In what way do they do it? Do they hold schools or do they drill individually, or do they teach?

There are two or three ways. One plan is that the officers of different regiments throughout the country belonging to the active militia shall go to the schools to live in barracks, and pass through the necessary course of study. Another plan is to send men from the permanent force to the officers because the best of our officers perhaps are those who are men actively engaged in civil life, and cannot afford to leave for four or six weeks, or even three weeks It always has been to some extent done, but it is proposed to do it more than ever; that competent teachers shall be sent from the permanent force to teach the officers at their own homes and, of course, in camp.
Is that the improved method of training and education recommended by Sir John French?

His reference there means up-to-date methods. For instance, Sir John French objected that, the old-time method of marching past and presenting arms and all that sort of thing was a waste of time, and that instead of that the men in the different regiments .should be taught the newer system/ of manoeuvres on a larger scale, conditions having entirely changed.
Will there be no marching past in future?

Not very much. The public are very much interested in the marching past, and they like to SDend a day in camp and see it, and it

will be continued for one day or so in the year, but to nothing like the extent it used to be.

House in committee on Bill (No. 170), to incorporate the New Ontario and Quebec Railway Company.-Mr. Gordon (Nipis-sing).
On section 1,

This Bill raises the very-much discussed question of provincial rights, but it goes a good deal further, in the sense of having much less excuse for being brought into this parliament, than any other Bill that I have seen here, with the exception, perhaps, of one or two waterpower Bills which have been much discussed. The purpose of the Bill is to incorporate a company professedly to build a railway from just outside the limits of the province of Ontario, in the province of Quebec at Lake Abitibi, across the northern part of Ontario for about 160 miles, traversing that part of northern Ontario which is being developed in the matter of railways by the government of Ontario at great expense to the people of the province, and by a policy which is just in its infancy, but in which a large amount of the assets of the province is involved. This professed main line, if it can be called such, does not traverse any part of the province of Quebec, and is practically of no use to that province. It is apparently put into the province of Quebec just as an excuse for this company coming to this parliament to get a charter. Then it proceeds 160 miles into that part of northern *Ontario which is being developed at great expense to the people of Ontario by the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, which is a people's railway, projected for and by the people for that purpose. The object of this company is manifest, I think, from the fact that it asks authority to build two little branch lines, one running northeast and southwest, and the other north and south, right in the territory traversed by the Timiskaming and Northern, each of these lines being only 25 miles in length. Evidently that is the whole purpose of this railway company. If a charter should be granted for these two little lines, it should be got from the Ontario legislature. Under subsection 10 of section 92 Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
of the British North America Act provincial legislatures have full power in regard to the following matters:
Local works and undertakings, other than such as are of the following classes:
(a.) Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province.
(b.) Lines of steamships between the province and any British or foreign country.
(c.) -Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
Unless some of these conditions exist, the province has full power to incorporate a company for building these railways. A representative of the Ontario government appeared before the Railway Committee when this Bill was under consideration there, and stated that the Ontario government objected to this road being built, believing that it was not bona fide in regard to the so-called main line of 160 miles, and they asked for some guarantee that that line was going to be built. No guarantee was forthcoming other than the statement that the company intended to build it. It struck me that there was a guarantee that could be given, and I have therefore, given notice of an amendment which I will move if the committee thinks the Bill should pass at all. In these matters it is surely up to us to find out what the bona fides of a railway company are. We are surely not going to give a company a charter to build a railway through one province just from the threshold of another, if they _ do not intend to build it, but if they are simply using it as an excuse for getting a charter to build a provincial road. If this company, under the pretense of building an interprovincial railway, while intending to build only two little bits of railway wholly in the province of Ontario, secure a charter from this parliament, and then never build the road which alone gives them a right to come here, they would in that way perpetrate what is virtually a fraud both on this parliament and on the provincial legislature. If the House is with me in that view, it will not pass this Bill. But if it does not go with me that far, then when we come to section 7 I will move my amendment, which is to the effect that the company shall not be allowed to build these little roads unless they first build the so-called main line. If they are not going to build that Toad, they should not have the charter from this parliament. If they are going bona fide to build it, they should not object to my amendment.

On section 7,

I should like to hear the hon. gentleman who is in charge of this Bill make some answer to the remarks that have just been made by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). We have here a main line which may be of very considerable importance, and we have two short lines which can be of no use, I think, to this Dominion, so far as public service is concerned, unless the main line is built. I would like to know why there should not be a provision here that they might make the two short lines or branches after they have completed the main line. We ought to have some explanation of that.

The member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), was speaking when I came in, and I inferred from his remarks that his principal trouble was that he is afraid that the people who are at the back of this railway are not going to build it. Now, if they are going to build the main line and also these branches, *1 presume he would have no objection. He stated, I think, that the Ontario government required some kind of a guarantee that these people would go on and build this road. I would like to know what kind of a guarantee they should give other than asking for this charter. These people intend to build both the main line and the branches, and I think it is better to allow them to build either their branches or the main line, whichever they choose to build first, whichever will be most advantageous to themselves. I think if the member for Lincoln knew as well as I do how badly railroads are needed in that country, and what a great advantage they would be, instead of opposing a Bill like this, he would do everything he could to further it. I may say for his information, as well as for the information of the House, that the country up there is a great agricultural country, and unless it is developed by railroads it will remain as it always has been, of no use to any person. I think this is a very important road, and should be built. I have heard no good reason given why the branch lines should not be included, and certainly I have heard from the hon. member for Lincoln no good reasons for objecting to this Bill.

I thought I had made it quite clear that I was contending for a different thing entirely from what the hon. gentleman has spoken of. I did not contend that this road should not be built, I only said that I wanted to be sure that this was not a trick played upon us by pretending to build a main line which they did not intend to build, and building the
branches first and stopping there. I did not say the road was not needed, I do not want to retard railway development. But I want to make sure that this whole road is going to be built, and I want the big part of the road to be built first before the branches are built, because the branches, if built alone, are purely provincial matters and are to connect with a purely provincial railway. This Bill provides that the road is to be built from a point on the National Transcontinental railway in the province of Quebec, and then southerly around the east end of upper Lake Abitibi, which is in the province of Ontario, a total distance of 160 miles, and all in the province of Ontario except two or three miles. '
If the promoters are sincere and intend building the whole of the railway, they will show their sincerity toy accepting the amendment I am about to propose. I am heartily anxious to help them to build the whole of the road but do not want them never to touch the main line of 160 miles, which might be of some use to the Dominion as a Dominion road, and content themselves with building these two little branch lines of 25 miles each. The most vicious interference with provincial rights would be to incorporate a little railway 25 miles long, purely provincial, to connect with another provincial railway, a railway provincially owned, and in no sense under the control of this parliament. If the company want a charter for those two branch lines, they can get it from the Ontario legislature. Surely we are not doing a wise thing in incorporating against the protest of the province of Ontario, two little bits of provincial railway of 25 miles each to connect with a provincially owned and controlled railway. I beg therefore to move the following amendment to be inserted as section 2:
2. The powers of construction granted by paragraphs (b) and (c) of this section shall not be exercised until the line of railway authorized by paragraph (a) shall have been constructed to the respective junctions on that line to which the lines authorized by said paragraphs (b) and (c) are to extend-

The same argument which my hon. friend has used now was used in the Railway Committee, and the committee' decided that as this was a peculiar section of country, and very probably the road would be built largely in the mining interests, we should give the company a charter. This is a peculiar section of the country,, and it is very probable that these branch lines may require to be built first to accommodate people settling there. Therefore, the Railway Committee saw fit to give-the charter to build the branch lines first-

There are two arguments of which I am growing tired. One is that we have done a thing before, and therefore must do it again. The other is that a thing has been done in a committee, and therefore must be adopted in this House. In the committee we are told that a thing has been done before, and that is given as an excuse why we should do it again,-no question *whether it is right or wrong, but only that it was done before-

If the hon. gentleman will allow me, I did not say that it should be done because it had been done before.
.Mr. BARKER. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesibitt) said that it 'had been done in committee and therefore we should do it here.
That is what I said.

The argument is precisely the same. Now, we have here a system of responsible government. It is useless for the _ ministers to profess that they are responsible only for government measures. Everybody knows that the ministry is responsible for the legislation of this House. Session after session we are deliberately violating the constitution of Canada, and the government know it. It is not done in so many words, but it is done. What would be said if I introduced a Bill in this House to construct a railway from Labrador to the western coast ot British Columbia, with power at any or every point along that distance to construct twenty-five mile branches? Would not the allegation that such a thing was reasonable be something such as you would address to the occupants of a madhouse? But what worse would that be than what we have here? The gentleman asks a charter to run a line from one province to another, with two branches. And he objects-and it is important for members of the House to consider whether this shows good faith or bad faith-he objects to a clause being put in that he shall not make the branches until he has made the main line. What can more clearly show that this is an attempt to evade the constitution ? Why the veriest simpleton in the country will understand that 'he wants the right to build the branches, and that is all he cares about. We have the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) here. I believe that he_ is trying to improve the railway law of this Dominion, and I think he has already done a great deal to improve that law. I ask him, what does he think of this deliberate, this evidently wilful and intentional attempt to break through the constitution? I have no interest in this matter. and do not know anybody connected with the company. But I appeal to the
Mr. NESBITT
House to consider whether the man who promotes this Bill and professes to want to build a line from a point in Quebec to a point in Ontario with two branch lines, and says he must construct the branch lines first, is not deliberately trying to evade the provisions of the constitution. Are we in this House not to use common sense? Why do they try to evade the provisions of the constitution under which we live? I do not care a snap of my finger about the individual interest. The gentleman who is promoting this Bill is a friend of mine, and sits on our own side of the House. But I do not think that is a reason why I should act and vote contrary to the law of the land as I am asked to do. Why should not he put in a provision that if these parties want to build a branch line, they must make it a branch to an existing railway-that is they must build the trunk first, and then the branch?

I think it is a disgrace to the intelligence of this House for any member to talk in that way about something that, as I believe, he does not know much about. Suppose the Transcontinental railway were completed from the junction to mileage 940, and not completed to mileage 1,000. And suppose one of these lines starts from one mileage, and the other from the other mileage, would there be common sense in the builders of the roads hauling stuff 60 miles by team to commence the building of another road? Is it not common sense to begin building a road from a point at which you have railway communication?

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gordon, Nipissing) wants an answer, this is the answer:	There is a
good deal less sense in parliament deliberately granting a charter under pretense of it being a Dominion railway, for two 25 mile roads that are entirely in Ontario. The hon. gentleman has not yet learned that the province of Ontario has power to incorporate railway companies. He proceeds entirely on the argument that if you do not hold a Dominion charter you have to haul stuff by horses. He does not know that Ontario has power to build railways, to build auy railway entirely within the limits of the province and neither does he know that if the railway is entirely within the limits of the province this parliament has no jurisdiction to incorporate it at all. The hon. gentleman had better ask leave to withdraw this Bill, communicate with the promoters, and suggest that they take the Bill before the provincial authorities. As my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) says, it makes no difference whether this road is five or 125 miles long, if it is entirely within the province. The hon. gentleman promoting this Bill argues

that he must have the right to build these two little branch lines-he calls them branch lines although I believe they constitute the only road that will ever be built -that he must be allowed to build a road 25 miles long, but he does not realize that if they are in the province of Ontario not only is the province of Ontario the power to iauthorize their building, but this parliament has no power to authorize them to do anything. I repeat my hon. friend can do everything that- he wants to do, without horses, without an automobile, without carts, under a provincial railway charter, and if my hon. friend knows that, probably he will see the necessity of accepting the suggestion, or else going to the province of Ontario, and getting his charter to build this line in all 50 miles long, which is entirey within the province of Ontario.
Carried.

I think we should have some idea from the minister how he views this matter. This may have to be a precedent. The House will have to decide upon this on the third reading. We cannot allow it to go through in a casual way, the House will have to take the responsibility ultimately, and if four other hon. gentlemen will stand up with me on the third reading we will divide upon it. I think the minister ought to say what the policy of the government is with reference to railways of this kind.

I am interested in this discussion, because this is the first I have heard of this Bill. I confess I do not know much about it, because I was not in the committee. I hardly understand that it is divided into a main and two. branch lines; it is Tather divided into three sections. As a matter of practical railway construction I could understand a situation where it would be wise and, from a practical construction point of view, absolutely necessary to build the branch first.

Is>
there any pretense of that here?

I do not know; I am trying to get information. The Timiskam-ing and Northern Ontario railway is not a branch of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but it will serve my illustration very well. It would have been very difficult on one section of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific to get supplies in if we had not had the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to take them up. That branch, it we might call the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario a branch for the moment, was constructed before the Grand Trunk Pacific. If it had all been under one charter I imagine the construction company would have built that branch before attempting to construct the main line, in
order to carry in its supplies. I could understand a situation where the cost of a railway could be materially reduced by building a branch line first in order to get the supplies, in. I do not know whether that is the situation in this case or not.
I am afraid that I am somewhat of a sinner-if sinner it can be called-in leaning to the view that it is better in the interests of the people and in the interests of transportation to have as many railways as possible under federal jurisdiction. I have had some experience during the last year. We have some railways under provincial	jurisdiction-I
am not speaking particularly of the province of Ontario now-to which the federal parliament has given _ aid. There is one case I have in my mind where a railway became so badly out of repair that it could not be operated and operations ceased. The rails were actually taken up, and there seemed to be no power on earth to stop the taking up and carting away of these rails by the owner of the road, although this parliament had given possibly $6,000 a mile towards the construction of the road. I am_ introducing legislation now with the object of effecting a remedy in such cases, but I found, in endeavouring to draw a clause, that we have no power within this parliament to deal with any road except those operating under a charter granted by the federal authority, or which has passed into the hands of a company that derives its power from the federal authority. That is one reason why I am very anxious to have all the railways possible brought under federal jurisdiction if it can he done without straining the constitution to the breaking point.
Why to the breaking point?
Where is the breaking point?
I believe the constitution was devised for the good of the people.
As the fellow says, ' which people,' the provincial people or the Dominion people?

All the people. I think that the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada is the best machinery to be found in the world for the control of railways. I do not think it has an equal anywhere, and I think I am serving the interest of the people if I can get as many railways as possible under that jurisdiction. Take this railway, for instance, I see the view point of my hon. friend, and I do not like to think that we are being deceived in granting a charter for some line that there is no intention of constructing, but that the charter is merely to be used for the

construction of two small lines. It is not in my recollection that we have ever challenged the bona tides of a company when it places a plan before us which shows an interprovincial line, or when it gives good reasons why the line should come under federal jurisdiction. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), says that the application for the charter is fraudulent. I would not like to go that far. Perhaps I am too kind hearted, but I always give a fellow the benefit of the doubt, till I prove that he is wrong.
It does not look it if he does not accept my amendment.

That may be the judgment of some, but perhaps the promoter says that he proposes to build the whole of the line covered by his charter, but it may be more convenient perhaps for financial reasons, or in connection with construction to build one of the proposed branch lines first, in order to facilitate the construction of the main line. The Bill can not get through to-night, and I will have an opportunity to look into it. I do not know anything about it, I was not at the committee, and I always hesitated to go against the finding of a committee particularly when I was not there and when I am not in as good a position to express an opinion as those who were present.
The attendance at the committee was small, the yeas and nays were not taken but the majority was very close for carrying the Bill and rejecting the amendment.
My memory is that there were only one or two against it.

It is neither polite nor fair for t'he hon. member to say that. I moved the amendemnt and half a dozen spoke in favour of it, and they certainly would have voted as they spoke, but as no vote was taken we cannot prove to a demonstration what the vote was. My hon. friend is entirely w^rong in saying' there were only one or two against it.

Surely the Minister of Railways is not to set up his individual opinion against the clear terms of the British North America Act. If a railway asks a charter from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and wanted 25 miles in every province over that distance, surely the hon. gentleman would not force on parliament his individual opinion that the federal authority should take everything it could under its jurisdiction.

If my hon. friend's illustration were carried out he would get into a position where he would have no jurisdiction constitutionally or in any other Mr. GRAHAM.
way. As the Dominion we have jurisdiction in every province.

The contention of the hon. minister in this respect is not in accordance with the clear terms of the constitution.
The order for private Bills having expired, the House resumed in Committee of Supply.

I wish to make one or two more observations to conclude my general remarks with reference to the reorganization under Sir John French's scheme. This reorganization will not result in any considerable increase in the votes of money required; in fact, it will not result in any increase whatever. During the three years past and the present year the estimates show practically no increase whatever. It is proposed to carry out the general scheme of reorganization without materially increasing the vote. For the past six or seven years we have had an annual vote of about $1,300,000 for the purpose of purchasing equipment of various kinds, including artillery, saddlery, rifles, &c., and it is proposed under this scheme of Sir John French to go on at precisely the same rate. We will increase the artillery and cavalry-the only two branches of the service to be increased- precisely as we are able to purchase the necessary equipment with the annual vote of $1,300,000. That is the only other general observation I have to make with regard to the proposed reorganization.

A great many people in Ontario have been anxious to know how far the report of Sir John French went. Was it with regard to a general reorganization or with regard to the personnel of the militia. Did he express any opinion as tc, the rank and file, as to the regimental officers, and as to the higher staff?

Sir John French spoke very highly of the rank and file; he spoke very highly of the officers; he spoke particularly well of the artillery; he was not so well pleased with the cavalry or with the infantry. But, on the whole, I think it is fair to say that he considered, in view of the short time of the annual drill, that the Canadian militia made a very good showing, and that with some changes which he suggested-some of which we can carry out, and some of which we will not be able to carry out-an effective force may be hoped for within a reasonable time.
Will the 3rd New Brunswick Regiment of Artillery drill this year?
Yes.
There must be some misunderstanding about that.
It was to have been disbanded, but I understand it is to be reorganized before the annual camp this year.
What is to be reorganized?
The battery to which my hon. friend refers.

They do not require any reorganization. I do not suppose there is a corps in the whole Dominion of Canada that is in better condition and has had better report for efficiency than the 3rd Regiment of Artillery. It has had a high record for years, and why this corps should have been dropped from the list of those to be drilled this year, I do not understand. Evidently the commanding officer has come to the conclusion, I presume with some good reason, that his corps was not to be drilled this year, and I shall read the order he issued.
3rd 'New Brunswick' Regiment, Canadian Artillery- Regimental orders by Lieut.-Col. John B. M. Baxter, commanding.
St. John, N.B., May 4, 1911.
1.	In view of the fact that this regiment has not yet been ordered to perform annual training this year it is desirable that its organization should be preserved intact and that all ranks should endeavour, by the exercise of voluntary spirit, to maintain the corps in the state of efficiency which has been its pride for years.
2.	The .first battery of artillery in St. John was founded 118 years ago to-day. Since that time the artillery organization in this city and province has been continuous, and since 1860 there has not been a year when the regiment has not been on parade.
3.	Under these circumstances the O.C. the regiment desires that all ranks shall join in performing voluntary drill during the coming season, paying particular attention to infantry drill and ceremonial, as the regiment will probably have several opportunities of appearing in public. It is to be distinctly understood that no one has authority to promise that any pay will be granted for the services so performed.
4.	Roll books of attendance will be kept posted as usual. Recruits who are willing to serve on these terms will be accepted. 0. C.'s batteries will make the usual arrangements for drill nights and other details.
5.	The N.C.O.'s and men are particularly reminded that they are not in any way released from their obligation to serve in the militia by reason of the corps not being ordered to perform annual training. Any who may wish to join or serve in any other corps may apply for discharge in the usual way.
6.	All ranks are specially reminded that it is not consistent with discipline in any way to criticise the action of their military superiors.
7.	The officers of the regiment will attend a special service at St. Paul's church on the
day of His Majesty's coronation. The hour, to be named afterwards, will be as nearly as possible that of the ceremony in Westminster Abbey. Full dress will be worn.
By order.
Major, Adj., 3rd Regt. C.A.
The name of the adjutant is not given here. It is quite evident from that order, issued by the commanding officer of this corps, that he must have had reason for believing that his corps was not going to perform annual drill this year. I do not know when the orders for annual drill are issued, but I presume that it has been customary to issue them previous to the present date. Of course, if the minister states that the corps is to drill, this adjutant must be labouring under a considerable misapprehension, and I would be glad to hear from the minister that the corps will be on the roster for drill as it always has been. While on my feet I would like to remind the minister that this corps is one of 1 think only three in the whole Dominion of Canada which, while it has been thoroughly efficient for years, a corps in which I take a great interest myself, having belonged to it for over twenty years, and one which I think stands as well on the records made by the inspectors who have inspected the various regiments as any corps in the Dominion, appears to be picked out in some way, so that it has not even one representative officer, non-commissioned officer or man-on the contingent which is to be taken to the coronation. I think there is good reason to ask the minister why this corps should not be granted the same privilege, if it is to be called such, that is given to every other corps, I believe, in the Dominion. If my memory serves me, the minister stated in his place in this House that there would be one representative of every corps in the Dominion in that coronation contingent. This corps, although it was asked to name one from each battery, named the men, but none has been chosen.

The com mittee will of course understand that it is impossible for me to keep in touch with the doings of each one of the 150 or 200 corps throughout the Dominion. I know Colonel Baxter, who is one of the most enthusiastic and keenest officers in Canada, and is a personal friend of my own. I am rather surprised, if matters are in the melancholy condition in which my hon. friend from St. John paints them, that Colonel Baxter had not intimated the fact to me, because he has not hesitated in the past, when he thought things were not being done as they ought to be done, to ask my direct intervention, and I have had the very great pleasure on more than one occasion of giving it. I did not know until

my hon. friend mentioned the fact that there was any difficulty of any kind with the 3rd Battery in so far as the coronation contingent is concerned. I shall be greatly surprised if it turns out that this regiment was not asked to send men. There were no non-commissioned officers invited to be sent; but men were to be chosen from every corps according to a certain rule laid down, and from those men, when they assemble at Quebec, non-commissioned officers will be selected. I will look into that matter at once. The selection of officers is an entirely different matter. We have about 40 officers to select from the active militia of Canada out of over 3.000 and from between 100 and 200 different corps, so that it is absolutely out of the question that we should select an officer from every corps or from perhaps one in ten.
The minister mistakes me if he thinks I made any such suggestion.
I understood my hon. friend to say that this is one of the few corps which have been slighted in the selection of officers.
As far as having any representative either officer, non-commissioned officer or man.

As to the men; I agree that the matter must be investigated, but as to officers not at all. The province of New Brunswick has the very great honour of supplying the commandant of the coronation contingent. When I made up an estimate of the number of officers which should be sent from each province, it was then decided that the number from New Brunswick would be two. Colonel Maclean was selected as commandant, and Captain MacKee of the New Brunswick artillery was selected.
What for?
The Moncton battery.
How long has that been m existence?
I do not know. He was selected because he had distinguished himself in South Africa, and wore the South African medal. He was selected by General Drury, who commands the maritime provinces.
What will the minister do with regard to having a representative from that corps on the contingent?
Is my hon. friend sure that the colonel of that regiment was not asked to select men for the coronation contingent?
I have my information direct from the colonel himself.
That he was not asked to do it?

That he was asked to name three men, one from each battery, and that he did so, but that not one of them was selected. He felt, and the whole corps feel, that they have been slighted. I believe I am correct in saying that the minister declared it was the intention that each corps should have a representative, in which case this corps is an exception, and some explanation is due.
It is not an exception, and my hon. friend has admitted that the colonel was asked to make a selection. If he did not make any, that was his fault.

My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) is under some misapprehension. I was told this evening by Colonel Baxter that he had been asked by the department to select men to go on the contingent, but that not seeing his regiment's name in the general order, he thought that had been cancelled. I asked him why he did not bring the matter to the attention of the department, and he said that he intended to do that today. but was not able to see the proper officer.

I am not labouring under any misapprehension at all, though my hon. friend may be. I am simply repeating the statement that the colonel made to me. If he has found out something else since, I did not know it. He told me that no man had been selected from his corps to go on the contingent.
Although he had sent in the names?
He named one from each of the three batteries, and those names were sent in. But not one of them was selected.
No notices have been sent out to the men who have been selected from the different corps, but I understand they will be sent out in a day or two.
If one of those men be selected, that will be satisfactory.
I have no doubt but that the three men have been selected, and are going on the contingent.
There are some others of us who may have some little discussion with the minister on this subject, and perhaps we might take up this item and resume the discussion on some other item.

There will be a special item brought down on Monday to provide the necessary money t# take the contingent to England, and that will be a very convenient time to discuss the coronation contingent generally.
What about the annual drill?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That will come up more appropriately on resolution 81.

The minister has made
a general statement, and there is a good deal of matter which we want to discuss in a general way.

I would suggest that we might pass a few items and allow any discussion concerning them on any other item. There is one item, that of the annual drill, which I want carried, as we cannot have our annual drill without it, and that drill will be coming on in a very few days.

We have no desire to make any obstruction to the providing of money for the annual drill of our militia. If the minister will undertake that any question regarding annual drill may be asked on any other item that will be satisfactory, and when we next go into committee we may discuss the general question and the minister's statement.
I would like item 80 passed as well, because that involves payment to officers in the active militia and is connected with the annual drill.
Is there any increase in these allowances this year?
I think not. There is a decrease of $15,000.

I would like to ask the hon. minister what considerations prompted him in making appointments to the coronation contingent from the 78th regiment in Pictou? And why Captain J. W. Macdonald, 78th regiment. I would like to know what prompted the minister to appoint this young man, who has not yet attained his majority, and was only appointed last fall to a commission.

The young gentleman served in camp last year, he had passed all his military examinations, and is well reported upon by his senior officer. And, so far as I know, he is an admirable representative of the 78th regiment. He certainly has the right name to entitled him to represent a highland regiment.

I would inquire further if, when this matter comes up on Monday,
we may discuss this aspect of the matter- a general discussion?
General discussion, of course.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 80 carry?

On that consideration. It is with great regret that I came downstairs to-night. I think that, under all the circumstances we might not have met at all this evening, considering that half the House, or nearly half-and the better half I may say-are employed so very pleasantly elsewhere. But I think we will give the minister all his annual drill vote if he will close up shop.

Quite satisfied.	-
